Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are proceeded with, I would like to ask when we shall be privileged to see a report of the last Imperial Conference. I presume that the notes have been extended; probably my right hon. friend has brought them back with him. Nothing could be of greater interest for us than to see exactly what has taken place at that important gathering. Also, will we

have a full report of all the proceedings of the conference, and not, as in the last instance, a very much reduced report for most of us, while a privileged few saw a verbatim Teport of all the proceedings. In this instance the conference is not one of a special nature, a conference of defence, but a general conference, and I hope we shall have the full report.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I hope the same thing, and I suppose the report will be published at an early day. I understand that it is now in the hands of the printer.
What printer -of this House?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. It is printed in England and is to be distributed as soon as it is printed.

Of course, it is very difficult to get any general supply if we are to rely on the British bluebook. 1 think on some occasions at least the book has been printed here in order that members of this House and of the Senate might have full information of what has taken place. Has the Prime Minister taken that into consideration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: On previous occasions we have had it reprinted, and there is no objection, if it is so desired, that it should be reprinted this time. I have nothing in my hand. The report is in the hands of the printer, and I expect it from day to day. We shall have a certain number of copies for distribution here and if they are not sufficient, we may have to reprint the report.
I think the document has been printed in Great Britain, because a copy came to hand to-day I do not know from what source it came.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The proceedings of the conference were printed from day to day, but the report is not finally struck until it is revised by each member of the conference. I sent my proof sheets just before I left England.
The document to which I allude purports to be a report of the conference. I do not know whether it has been revised or not, but it has an index of the various subjects at the commencement.

I understood, from what appeared in the newspapers since my right hon. friend returned, that a copy had reached this country, that my right hon. friend in fact had brought back with him a. report of the conference, and I am a little anxious to know if we have to wait for the printing in England.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sorry to say that, as often happens, my hon. friend has been misinformed. I brought nothing back from the conference; I am no more privileged in that respect than my hon. friend. All I saw was the proof sheets and my last proof sheet was sent to the printer the day before I left England.

May I ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) if it is correct that there are still out of employment a large number of the men connected with the recent strike on the Grand Trunk railway, and is it my hon. friend's intention to communicate to the House the report of Judge Barron in regard to that strike?

A few days ago I communicated with Mr. Hays, asking if Judge Barron's report had been received, and what action he proposed to take on the report. In a letter of June 26, Mr. Hays replied
As to the investigation conducted by IDs Honour Judge John Barron, at my request, will say, he has concluded his report, but it is very lengthy, consisting of several hundred pages of testimony, and I have not as yet been able to thoroughly consider it. I may add, however, that any recommendations therein will receive our most careful and favourable consideration.
Mr. Hays further intimates that he has made a similar intimation to the representatives of the employees who have been communicating with him.
That is not quite an answer to my question. What 1 would like to know is whether the members of the House will have an opportunity of examining that report?

The report is not made to parliament or government. It is a report made to Mr. Hays himself. I cannot say whether Mr. Hays intends to make the report public or not. I have no assurance from him on that point.
The other question my hon. friend has overlooked, as to how many of the men are still out of employment.
I understand that there are several. I could not give the exact number.
What is my hon. friend doing towards getting these men reinstated, as he took an active part in the settlement?
The government has kept in touch with the company, and has intimated to it that it hopes that it will see its way to reinstate any man who may still be out.
Has anything been done by my hon. friend or his department since the adjournment of the House a few weeks ago?
Yes. The communication which 1 have just read is an answer to a communication which I sent to Mr. Hays; and other officers of the company have been communicated with as well.

Before the orders of the day are called I would like to inform my right hon. friend in connection with what I mentioned a moment ago, that the document to which I alluded yesterday seems to be a report of the proceedings of the recent Imperial Conference. It is a blue-book entitled ' Imperial Conference 1911;' precis of the proceedings presented to both Houses of parliament, by command of His Majesty, June, 1911, printed by the government printers; and it begins with the proceedings on the 1st day, Tuesday 2Srd May, 1911, on which day a resolution was passed presenting a humble address of the conference to His Majesty, and it ends with a record of the proceedings on the 20th June, 1911, setting forth the concluding speeches of certain members of the conference.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When was it presented to parliament?

June, 1911, the day of the month is not mentioned. The conference seems to have come to the conclusion, according to this document, on the 20th of June, and evidently was presented to parliament some time between the 20th and the end of June.

No one who has been in that locality. as I have been, could fail to be impressed with the conviction that no stone should be left unturned in order to help these people out. Many sad cases have I witnessed, cases of heart-rending misery, but I shall not attempt to enter into details because you have had that information already through the press. I am glad, however, to find that the loss of life will not be as great as we feared. Up to Monday, so far as I could ascertain, 63 corpses had been recovered, and many people who were thought to have been lost are continually being found out at other points. There is no doubt, however, that the loss of life was considerably more than can be judged by the number of bodies which have been recovered.
I have information from the clerk of the town of Cochrane that the last assessment of that town was $913,000. The rate of taxation was 25 mills on the dollar. The town owed $75,000. It issued debentures to the extent of $50,000, which have all been sold, and there is on hand about $40,000 in cash. The corporation loss through the destruction of town property was $21,000. The total insurance will only be in the vicinity of $200,000, while the total loss in Cochrane alone the assessor estimated at $2,000,000. In this condition of affairs, you can easily see that the town is in very bad shape for the purpose of rebuilding, because those who may go there to build will find themselves at once saddled with a very high taxation. I, therefore, am of the opinion that the government should at a very early date do- something towards relieving that town as a whole. For this we have a precedent created lately in the case of the conflagration nt Campbellton.
I would suggest, and I trust that the suggestion will meet with the approval of the government, that something substantial should be done in that connection, and that a very liberal amount of cash should be at once provided to be handed over to a central committee for distribution throughout the district for the benefit of the settlers. In this one district I have spoken of in the townships of Capreol and Hanmer, of which we have heard very little in the papers, there are to-dav 25 families of settlers home-ltss and destitute. I am sure the government have this matter at heart, and" I simply urge them to make a liberal grant to alleviate the sufferings of these people.

I wish to endorse briefly what has been said by my hon. friend (Mr. Gordon, Nipissing). I come from a district somewhat south of the fire region, but many people from my own home town were unfortunately in that fire at Porcupine. I have their description of the scene there,

and of the results of the fire. Some few men are still undiscovered, and it is feared they have been lost in the fire. These towns are not in a position to help themselves, they have now large debts, they have been built up very quickly, and it is almost impossible to get new settlers to go in there, and assume the old debt created previous to the fire. It would be only reasonable that the government should do something to help out the corporations in that way. It is supposed too that a large number of men have been killed or burned in the woods and there is at present no means of searching for their bodies. Many sufferers from the fire are absolutely blind from the effect of smoke and heat, and some poor unfortunates thus afflicted may be still in the woods around that settlement. The Ontario government has been very generous in this matter, so far at least as the T'eni-iskaming and Northern Ontario railroad is concerned. They are moving the men out free of charge, and carrying in supplies free and in fact doing everything possible to help the settlers. It is only right that this government should do as much for these people as they have done for settlers in foreign countries, as-, for instance, at the time of the earthquakes in San Francisco and Italy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will only remind the hon. gentlemen that this matter was brought up in the House yesterday when a brief statement was made as to the action which the government had taken, and the present position of the whole matter. If my hon. friends will be good enough to read that statement they will see that the matter has already been engaging the attention of the government, and will engage their further attention.

I would ask the Minister of Labour when lie intends to bring down the report of the conciliation board appointed to enquire into the trouble between the miners and operators in southern Alberta and the Crowsnest district of British Columbia, and also what action is being taken or has been taken by the government since the reception of that report? I am sure that he as well as other members of the House recognize that each day the seriousness of the situation increases. In a very short time now we will have cold weather throughout the prairie provinces, and the railways will soon commence to move the large crop of grain so that all cars will be in use, and the difficulty of getting the necessary supply of coal through to the prairie provinces will be very great. Every day the seriousness of that danger increases. I saw it stated

in the press that the assistant to the hrst vice president of the Canadian *racific Railway had made the statement that undoubtedly numbers of settlers would be frozen to death . in the prairie provinces, unless some immediate relief was given. We have been inviting, and are taking in very large numbers of settlers, and it is important from every standpoint that there should be an ample supply of fuel. I have here a number of references t,o this matter from different western papers, most of them couched in very strong language indeed. If I read an extract or two I only do so to impress on the minister, and other members of the government how earnestly the western people feel in regard to this particular matter. Whether rightly or wrongly there is a strong feeling throughout the west that the government has not done its whole duty in this matter ; they feel that there has been unnecessary delay. It is true that, just before the recess, the minister of Labour (Hon. Mr. King), in reply to a question in the House, said that the government had offered their services, and he intimated further that it was possibly because neither the operators nor the miners desired publicity that they had, up to that time, refused to avail themselves of those services. I ventured at that time to state that it was possibly not from fear of publicity, but because they had lost confidence in the Lemieux Act that this refusal had been made. I think all subsequent events go to prove that the suggestion I made at that time was correct. Whatever has been the past history of the Lemieux Act in the settling of various disputes, certainly in this case it has been a lamentable failure in every particular. Instead of assisting in any way it has been the means undoubtedly of preventing both parties com-mg together because, relying on that Act, they have waited from day to day until it drifted from week to week, and finally into months before that report was completed.
I shall not criticise the members of that board nor their appointment, but I wish to read an editorial from one of the western papers, which I think voices largely the feeling and the sentiment of those people. As I say the language is strong, but it is because they feel very strongly on the matter, and feel, as I have said, that there has been neglect on the part of the government. This editorial which appears in the Calgary 'Herald,' is as follows:

If for no other reason than its deplorable handling of the coal strike the federal government should be rejected and condemned by the people of western Canada. It is not only that the Department of Labour has utterly failed to reach a settlement but also that it has displayed an indifference to the situation that is nothing else than shameful. Reciprocity versus anti-reciprocity is a debatable question, but the need for coal next winter-, and the suffering which will come to western Canada for lack of it, are not matters of debate but of common knowledge.
for nearly four months the mines of southern Alberta have been closed through a differ-en®e between employers and employed. After a delay that was in itself reprehensible, a con-eiuation board was organized and a man put at the head of it who, in the opinion of those best qualified to judge, has shown himself a lamentable failure.
Meanwhile, what of the young Minister of Labour who, when he was a deputy, used to go arouud hunting trouble in order that lie might settle it. Have the sweets of office clogged the wheels of his industry, or has he grown too great to hearken bo a public cry? In the press dispatches we read that Mr. Gordon's report has at least reached Ottawa, but that it cannot be opened until Mr. Mackenzie King chooses to come back and do so, while we also read that Mr. King is delivering political speeches before a Quebec audience. What cares he for Alberta and Saskatchewan ? A minister of the Crown must not be bothered with trifles.
And here in the west are a million of people who will suffer because of Mr. King's selfish carelessness and Mr. Gordon's laziness. Here homes are without coal, here manufactories are hampered for lack of fuel. Here the steam ploughs on which the development of our country largely depends have had to cease operations on account of the strike. Here we have three great provinces whose people depend on coal for their winter warmth, and we know that however the strike is now settled there will he suffering and privation in thousands upon thousands of western homes during the coming winter. Is it not scandalous that a lazy and surfeited government should sit calmly by and watch its people robbed of the use of their natural heritage? Such a strike as this first impels one to believe that all coal mines should be controlled and operated by the government. But on the other hand if the government were as inefficient as the Department of Labour ha® shown itself to be, the last stage might prove to he worse than the first.
Then there is a long article in another paper, in even stronger language, which perhaps I had better not read.
Read it.

This is from the Lethbridge ' Daily News,' a paper published in the centre of the affected district. I will read an extract.
Must the coal mining industry of this country be tied up to suit the convenience of the cocksure and bumptious youth who presides over the Department of Labour?
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I am not responsible for this language, but I trust the minister will thoroughly understand it.
The interests of thousands of people, the lives of some of them, perhaps, are at stake. Already there has been great inconvenience if

The merchants in the affected districts need the money for the goods that they have supplied the miners. Must all of these multifarious interests languish because Mackenzie King is an Berlin gratifying his vanity and boring bis constituents.
The Lemieux Act specifically states that as soon as the award reaches Ottawa it shall he made public and that a copy be given to any newspaper in Canada that asks for it. H e Terp representative at Ottawa has made this request and no doubt all of the other newspaper representatives have done the same, but Mr. King is not at home.
I admit that the language I have read is somewhat strong, and I have only read these editorials from western papers because they are published in this immediate district, and I think correctly reflect the views of the people of that district. Some portions of the affected districts are in my own riding of Kootenay. There are three great smelters depending on the output of coal from the district. They consume probably on the average 150 tons a day., or 34,500 tons a month. One of these has been shut down for some time; fortunately the others, by making an arrangement with the transportation company for a special rate, have been enabled to import coke from Pennsylvania and to continue running. How long that condition will last, they are unable to say. If, as is more than likely, the fight continues much longer, and they also are compelled to shut down, then many other dependent industries will be closed, and many more thousands of men, just at the season when work is most needed, will be thrown out of employment. For these reasons I think that the Department of Labour should inform the House and the country what steps they are taking to bring about a settlement of these difficulties.

Through the courtesy of my hon. friend in communicating his intention to bring up this subject in the House to-day, I am able to hand him a copy of the report of the board which has investigated this dispute. I may say by way of explanation as to why a copy was not laid on the table before, that it is not customary to lay copies of reports of Boards of Conciliation on the table of the House: they are given out to the press as soon as received, and they are also published in the ' Labour Gazette.' But it has not been a customary procedure to lay them on the table of the House. However, I am glad to present this report to the House, though it has already been published in large part in the press, and I have no doubt the details are familiar to, my hon. friend.

I must say that I expected, when my hon. friend began his remarks, that he would deal with this question from the point of view of the interests concerned, and the public welfare, and that he would not have introduced into the discussion editorials from party journals that have been written certainly for political purposes, and not to alleviate the situation in the west at the present time. If there is one thing above another which to my mind, is all important in connection with the western situation at the present time, it is that it should not he made a matter of party politics. The moment it is attempted to make political capital out of the serious industrial situation in the west at the present time, that moment the difficulty of settlement is going to become increased, and a heavy onus will rest upon those who take that course in approaching this question. The government, through the Department of Labour, has tried to deal with this question in a fearless and a direct manner. When the cessation of operations took place, the first step taken was to endeavour to get the parties to agree to allow the dispute to be investigated, so that the public might know what were the causes of the dispute, and what would be a fair basis of settlement. As a result of the method by which the department approached the question at that juncture, we were able, without any act of compulsion, to get the parties voluntarily to agree to refer the matter to a board. I admit that it took a little time. But I may say that any other method would not have accomplished the result at all, that the parties would not have willingly referred their differences to a board if we had tried to coerce them. By adopting the method of voluntary conciliation, we were successful in getting the parties to go before a board, and in having a hoard investigate the conditions. That board has gone into the matter fully, and the report which has been presented by the board gives to the public I think an intelligent idea of the causes which are at the bottom of this dispute. It does more than that, it outlines what, in the opinion of the hoard, appears to he a fair basis of settlement of the dispute. It is true that it has taken the board a considerable time to get through its work; but hon. gentlemen must remember that the dispute in British Columbia and Alberta at the present time is one of the largest mining disputes that has ever taken place on this continent. There are some 18 different mining companies affected; there are 18 locals oAhe United Mine Workers affected. The dispute is not one which could have been dealt with quickly, if it were to he dealt with intelligently and thoroughly.

The chairman of the board has very wisely taken the view that if this western situation is to be satisfactorily solved at all it will not be by going superficially into the matter, but by investigating the difficulty thoroughly and giving to the public as full an account of the situation as it is possible to give, at the same time making recommendations which, in the light of all the information, he has reason to feel will furnish a fair basis of settlement The board's report has been given out. It is not unreasonable to hope that the parties, having before them the report of the board, although up to the present, they have not seen their way to reach a settlement, will now use that report as a basis for coming to an agreement.
Would the minister tell me when he received that report and when it was given to the press?
